usage: you stay, they go — the core contrast with 계세요
shop/airline staff to a departing guest; highest formality
go safely / take care on the way
warmer, caring variant — implies concern for the journey
used toward teachers, elders; a step above 조심히 가세요
examples: A: 이제 가 볼게요. / B: 네, 안녕히 가세요.
A: I'll head off now. / B: Take care, goodbye.
short everyday farewell — B stays while A leaves
손님, 안녕히 가세요. 또 오세요.
Goodbye, ma'am/sir. Please come again.
shop staff: 안녕히 가세요 pairs naturally with 또 오세요
선생님, 살펴 가세요. 안녕히 가세요.
Take care on the way, teacher. Goodbye.
student stays as the teacher leaves; 살펴 가세요 adds extra deference toward the departing senior
nuance: 안녕히 가세요 is the goodbye you say to the person who is LEAVING while you remain behind. 안녕(安寧) is Sino-Korean for 'peace, well-being'; 히 makes it adverbial ('peacefully'); and 가세요 is the polite imperative of 가다 'to go' — so the whole thing literally wishes them 'go in peace'. The decisive contrast is with its twin 안녕히 계세요 (계시다 'to stay/be [of a person]'): the verb alone tells you who moves. The English-speaker pitfall is huge — English 'goodbye' is a single phrase for both parties, so learners routinely fire 안녕히 가세요 at the person they are leaving behind, which sounds like ordering your host out of their own home. The one-second fix: if my feet are moving, use 계세요; if their feet are moving, use 가세요. For warmer farewells add 조심히 가세요 ('go carefully') or the more deferential 살펴 가세요 ('go with care') toward a teacher or elder. The most formal register, heard from shop or airline staff, is 안녕히 가십시오.

structuredNuance.t: Word by word: 안녕히 ('peacefully', from 安寧 'peace') + 가세요 ('please go', polite imperative of 가다). Real meaning: 'Goodbye' — said specifically to the person who is physically departing while you stay put. Not interchangeable with any other goodbye.

Use it whenever the OTHER person is leaving and you stay: at a shop door, at home after a guest departs, at work as a colleague heads out. Register: 가세요 is polite (해요체) — fine for most everyday situations including strangers and colleagues. Step up to 가십시오 for guests at formal establishments. Add 조심히/살펴 for warmth toward elders or teachers.

The twin is 안녕히 계세요: 가세요 (go) = they leave; 계세요 (stay) = you leave. 조심히 가세요 and 살펴 가세요 are emotional upgrades — they carry concern for the journey, not just a farewell. 잘 가요 exists but is very casual and somewhat blunt; 안녕히 가세요 is the neutral-polite standard.

안녕히 가세요 (polite) → 안녕히 가십시오 (very formal) → 조심히 가세요 (warm) → 살펴 가세요 (extra-deferential for elders). Casual versions: 잘 가요 (polite-casual), 잘 가 (반말, close friend). Adding 또 봐요 / 또 뵙겠습니다 turns it into 'see you again'.

English 'goodbye' carries no directional information — it works for both the leaver and the stayer. Korean forces you to choose: 가세요 if THEY go, 계세요 if YOU go. Firing 안녕히 가세요 at someone you are leaving behind sounds like you are kicking them out. Always check whose feet are moving first.

mistakes: Saying 안녕히 가세요 when YOU are the one leaving — it tells the person staying to 'go', which sounds like kicking them out of their own space; when you leave, say 안녕히 계세요 instead.
Treating English 'goodbye' as a single phrase for all situations — Korean forces a directional choice: 가세요 (they leave) vs 계세요 (you leave). Picking wrong is one of the most common beginner errors.
Writing 안녕이 가세요 — the adverb ending is 히, not 이: it is always 안녕히. 안녕이에요 is a completely different phrase ('it is okay / hello in text').

english: Goodbye (said by the person who is leaving).
usage: you leave, they stay — mirror image of 가세요
departing a formal setting such as an office or ceremony
softening phrase added before 안녕히 계세요 so leaving early reads polite
bye, keep up the good work
natural dual exit line when leaving a still-working colleague
examples: A: 먼저 가겠습니다. 안녕히 계세요. / B: 네, 안녕히 가세요.
A: I'll be heading off now. Goodbye (stay well). / B: Take care, goodbye.
A is leaving and says 안녕히 계세요 to B; B stays and returns 안녕히 가세요 — each uses the correct directional verb
저 먼저 갈게요. 안녕히 계세요.
I'm off first. Take care and stay well.
you depart while others stay; 먼저 갈게요 flags you are the first to leave
바쁘신데 시간 내 주셔서 감사합니다. 안녕히 계세요.
Thank you for making time despite being busy. Goodbye.
polite close of a meeting — you leave, your host remains
nuance: 안녕히 계세요 is the mirror image of 안녕히 가세요: you say it when YOU are the one leaving and the other person STAYS. The pivot is the verb — 계시다 is the honorific of 있다 'to be/remain (of a person)', so 계세요 wishes the one staying to 'remain in peace'. Both phrases share the same 안녕(安寧) 'peace' root; the verb alone signals direction. English speakers reliably swap the two because 'goodbye' has no who-moves information — the one-second fix is: if my feet are moving, use 계세요; if their feet are moving, use 가세요. A smooth social move before departing is to add 먼저 갈게요 or 먼저 가 볼게요 ('I'll head off first') so leaving ahead of others doesn't seem abrupt or rude. When leaving a workplace where colleagues are still working, pairing 안녕히 계세요 with 수고하세요 ('keep up the good work') is the natural and considerate exit. Formal register: 안녕히 계십시오.

structuredNuance.t: Word by word: 안녕히 ('peacefully') + 계세요 ('please stay/remain', honorific polite imperative of 계시다). Real meaning: 'Goodbye' — said by the person who is departing to the person left behind. The verb 계시다 is the honorific form of 있다 'to exist/stay', not 가다 'to go'.

Use whenever YOU are leaving and others remain: wrapping up a visit, leaving work, departing a class. Register: 계세요 is polite (해요체), suitable for most everyday contexts. Step up to 계십시오 for a very formal departure. In workplace settings, add 수고하세요 to acknowledge those still working. Pair with 먼저 갈게요 to soften leaving before others.

The twin 안녕히 가세요 is for the stayer, not the leaver. 수고하세요 is an add-on phrase, not a replacement — it acknowledges the work they continue, while 안녕히 계세요 is the farewell itself. 조심히 가세요 is for sending off someone else, not for when you yourself are departing.

안녕히 계세요 (polite) → 안녕히 계십시오 (very formal). Casual: 안녕히 계세요 already sounds somewhat formal in casual speech; close friends may just say 나 간다 ('I'm off') or 잘 있어 ('stay well', 반말). Common expansion: 먼저 가겠습니다 + 안녕히 계세요 + 수고하세요 — the standard graceful workplace exit.

English speakers reliably say 안녕히 가세요 as they walk out the door — which tells the people staying to leave. The fix is the same for both phrases: check whose feet are moving. Your feet moving = 계세요. Their feet moving = 가세요. Getting this backwards is one of the most embarrassing and common beginner farewell mistakes.

mistakes: Using 안녕히 가세요 as you walk out the door — that orders the people staying to leave; the person departing always says 안녕히 계세요.
Saying 안녕히 있으세요 with plain 있다 — to show respect for a person staying, you must use the honorific verb 계시다, so it is always 안녕히 계세요, never 안녕히 있으세요.
Bolting without a word in a group setting — add 먼저 갈게요 / 먼저 가 보겠습니다 before 안녕히 계세요 so leaving first feels considerate, not abrupt.

usage: warm, friendly-polite (해요체) — first encounter, any context
humble-polite; toward a senior or VIP you have long wanted to meet
standard echo reply — always mirror the same register
examples: A: 안녕하세요, 저는 소연이에요. / B: 만나서 반가워요!
A: Hello, I'm Soyeon. / B: Nice to meet you!
basic exchange at a first meeting — B reflects A's register
안녕하세요, 만나서 반가워요. 저는 지민이에요. 잘 부탁해요.
Hello, nice to meet you. I'm Jimin. Looking forward to working together.
greeting plus self-intro — 잘 부탁해요 anchors the relationship going forward
말씀 많이 들었어요. 만나서 정말 반갑습니다.
I've heard so much about you. I'm truly pleased to meet you.
formal introduction after someone has been spoken of — 정말 adds genuine warmth; 반갑습니다 lifts the register
nuance: 만나서 반가워요 = 만나서 ('upon meeting / because we've met', from 만나다+ the causal connector -아서) + 반가워요 (반갑다 'to be glad/delighted'). So it literally says 'I am glad because I have met you' — the emotion 반가움 is the point, not just a social formula. Note the grammar: 반갑다 is a ㅂ-irregular adjective, so before -아/어요 the ㅂ drops and becomes 우, giving 반가워요 (not 반갑어요) — the same shift as 춥다→추워요, 돕다→도와요. Register-wise, 반가워요 is warmly friendly; 반갑습니다 is buttoned-up formal for business and ceremonies; the humble 만나 뵙게 되어 반갑습니다 is reserved for high-respect encounters. A crucial situation note: 만나서 반가워요 is essentially a FIRST-MEETING expression. English speakers often reuse 'nice to see you' at subsequent meetings, but at second or third encounters Koreans naturally switch to 오랜만이에요 ('long time no see') or 잘 지냈어요? ('have you been well?'). Reusing the first-meeting phrase can imply you forgot meeting them. The standard reply to 반가워요 is 저도 반가워요.

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 만나서 ('because we've met') + 반가워요 ('I'm glad'). Real meaning: 'Nice to meet you' — but the emotion is genuine, not just polite noise. 반갑다 expresses actual delight at the encounter, so the phrase feels warmer than a robotic 'nice to meet you'.

Use specifically at a FIRST meeting — not at second meetings or reunions. 반가워요 (해요체) suits most peers and new acquaintances. 반갑습니다 (합쇼체) is for formal introductions — business, interviews. 만나 뵙게 되어 반갑습니다 is the high-respect form when meeting a senior or VIP for the first time.

만나서 반가워요 is for FIRST meetings. At later meetings after a gap, use 오랜만이에요 ('long time no see'). For a warm second greeting with no gap, 또 만났네요 ('we meet again') works. 반갑다 vs 좋다: 반갑다 is specifically about the joy of this encounter; 좋아요 just means 'good/I like it' and cannot replace 반가워요 in introductions.
반가워요 (short friendly form) → 만나서 반가워요 (full form) → 만나서 반갑습니다 (formal) → 만나 뵙게 되어 반갑습니다 (humble-formal). Casual 반말: 만나서 반가워. The ㅂ-irregular drill: 반갑다 → 반가워요, 반갑습니다 — never 반갑어요.

Two traps: (1) Re-using 만나서 반가워요 every time you see the same person — it's a first-meeting phrase; at reunions switch to 오랜만이에요 or 잘 지냈어요?, or you imply you forgot meeting them. (2) Pronouncing or writing 반갑어요 — the ㅂ-irregular rule makes it 반가워요; the wrong form marks a beginner immediately.

mistakes: Saying 반갑어요 — 반갑다 is ㅂ-irregular; the -어요 form is 반가워요 (ㅂ → 우). Writing or pronouncing 반갑어요 is a clear grammar error.
Re-using 만나서 반가워요 the second time you see the same person — it implies you forgot the first meeting; at reunions use 오랜만이에요 instead.
Replying with a bare 네 to someone's 반가워요 — always mirror warmly with 저도 반가워요 so the introduction doesn't feel one-sided.

english: How do you do (formal first meeting).
usage: very formal, humble — first meeting with a senior, executive, or client
how do you do, I'm Minsu Kim
standard opener that leads directly into your name and affiliation
it is an honor to meet you
elevated beyond 처음 뵙겠습니다 — toward a VIP or highly-respected person
I look forward to your guidance and cooperation
the near-obligatory closer after 처음 뵙겠습니다 in formal introductions
examples: A: 처음 뵙겠습니다. 한국 팀의 이소연입니다. / B: 네, 반갑습니다. 잘 부탁드립니다.
A: How do you do. I'm Soyeon Lee from the Korean team. / B: Pleased to meet you. Looking forward to working together.
formal business introduction — A uses the full humble opener; B replies with the standard formal reciprocal
처음 뵙겠습니다. 김민수입니다. 앞으로 잘 부탁드립니다.
How do you do. I'm Minsu Kim. I look forward to working with you.
complete three-part formal self-introduction: greeting + name + forward-looking closer
부장님, 처음 뵙겠습니다. 말씀 많이 들었습니다.
Director, how do you do. I have heard so much about you.
junior greeting a senior executive — the honorific 부장님 address plus 말씀 많이 들었습니다 shows you value the senior's reputation
nuance: 처음 뵙겠습니다 is the high-formality, humble greeting for meeting someone for the very FIRST time, reserved primarily for business, institutional, or high-respect personal encounters. Breaking it down: 처음 = 'first time / for the first time'; 뵙다 (also written 뵈다) is the HUMBLE SUPPLETIVE verb for 'to see/meet someone of higher status', the deferent counterpart of plain 만나다/보다 — by using 뵙다 you lower yourself before the other person. The 겠 here is not the future tense but a formal-softening modal that adds a sense of 'I shall / I am so honored to' — equivalent to 'I shall respectfully meet you (for the first time)'. Contrast with 만나서 반가워요: that phrase expresses your personal emotion (glad), while 처음 뵙겠습니다 expresses deference and institutional formality — they are often combined in sequence (처음 뵙겠습니다 → 반갑습니다). The English-speaker pitfall is using it with peers or friends, where it sounds absurdly stiff or even sarcastic ('oh, HOW do you do'). Save it strictly for clients, executives, in-laws at first meeting, or any high-stakes formal introduction. It almost always links to 잘 부탁드리겠습니다 / 잘 부탁드립니다 to close the introduction.

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 처음 ('for the first time') + 뵙겠습니다 ('I shall humbly see/meet you', humble-formal). Real meaning: 'How do you do' — a fixed formula of deference and formality for a first encounter with someone of higher or equal institutional standing. The humility is baked into the verb 뵙다.

Use ONLY in formal first meetings — business clients, executives, academic supervisors, in-laws, celebrities/VIPs, or formal institutional settings. It is NOT appropriate for peer introductions, casual acquaintance meetings, or any situation where the level of formality is moderate. Misuse with friends sounds theatrical and ironically disrespectful.

처음 뵙겠습니다 vs 만나서 반가워요: the former is deference-focused and registers-heavy; the latter is emotion-focused (glad) and polite-casual. 처음 뵙겠습니다 vs 만나 뵙게 되어 영광입니다: '영광 (honor)' escalates to VIP level. In practice, Koreans often sequence them: 처음 뵙겠습니다 → 반갑습니다 → 잘 부탁드립니다.

처음 뵙겠습니다 (standard formal) → 만나 뵙게 되어 영광입니다 (VIP level). After the first meeting, switch to 다시 뵙겠습니다 ('I'll see you again') or 또 뵙겠습니다. When they leave formal contexts: 처음 뵙겠습니다 + 자기소개 (name, affiliation) + 잘 부탁드립니다 is the canonical three-beat introduction.

Two traps: (1) Using it casually — among peers or friends it sounds stuffy or sarcastic. English 'nice to meet you' is register-neutral, but 처음 뵙겠습니다 is strictly high-formal. (2) Reusing it at a second meeting — 처음 means 'first time', so saying it again implies you forgot. Switch to 다시 뵙겠습니다 or 오랜만입니다.

mistakes: Using 처음 뵙겠습니다 with friends or peers — it is steep formal-humble language and sounds sarcastic in casual settings; among equals say 만나서 반가워요.
Misspelling or saying 뵈겠습니다 instead of 뵙겠습니다 — the set greeting is 뵙겠습니다; while 뵈다 and 뵙다 are related, the conventional frozen first-meeting formula uses 뵙겠습니다.
Reusing it on a second meeting — 처음 means 'first time', making it contradictory; switch to 또 뵙겠습니다 / 다시 뵙겠습니다 or 오랜만입니다.

english: I will eat well (said before eating).
usage: I'll eat well (= thanks for the food)
polite (합쇼체) — said just before eating, especially when someone cooked or is treating
softer polite version (해요체) — slightly less formal but still courteous
complimenting the cook in advance; warmer and more personal than bare 잘 먹겠습니다
adds explicit verbal gratitude — used when receiving a gift of food or a very generous meal
examples: A: 다 됐어요, 어서 드세요. / B: 잘 먹겠습니다!
A: It's ready, please eat. / B: Thank you for the food!
host invites, guest responds with the pre-meal phrase — the most common exchange at a Korean table
와, 맛있겠다! 잘 먹겠습니다.
Wow, looks amazing! I'll eat well.
casual delight before digging in — 잘 먹겠습니다 doubles as a food-appreciation comment
직접 차려 주셔서 감사합니다. 정말 잘 먹겠습니다.
Thank you so much for preparing all this yourself. I will truly eat well.
thanking a host who cooked — 정말 and 직접 (personally, by hand) add sincerity
nuance: 잘 먹겠습니다 is the fixed courtesy phrase said JUST BEFORE eating, particularly when someone has cooked for you or is treating you to a meal. Structure: 잘 'well' + 먹다 'to eat' + the forward-looking intention marker -겠- ('I shall / I intend to') + formal -습니다, so literally 'I shall eat well'. This is Korea's table-side 'thank you for the food' — functionally equivalent to itadakimasu in Japanese. The critical contrast is tense: -겠- looks forward, so 잘 먹겠습니다 is always PRE-meal; after finishing you switch to the past 잘 먹었습니다. Mixing these up (saying 먹겠습니다 after eating, or 먹었습니다 before) is the single most common learner error with this phrase pair. Register descends from formal 잘 먹겠습니다 → polite 잘 먹을게요 → casual 잘 먹을게 → very casual 잘 먹자 (proposing eating together). A warmer variant is 맛있게 먹겠습니다, which compliments the food or cook in advance. The English-speaker pitfall is taking it literally — it is NOT a boast about one's appetite, and you say it even for a tiny snack or a single bite someone offers you.

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 잘 ('well') + 먹겠습니다 ('I shall eat', with forward-looking -겠-). Real meaning: 'Thank you for the food / I'll eat well' — a fixed pre-meal courtesy ritual, not a statement about appetite. Said regardless of actual hunger or the size of the portion.

Say it the moment before picking up your chopsticks, especially when someone cooked or paid. Register: 잘 먹겠습니다 (합쇼체) is the default polite form — use it with anyone older, at restaurants when treated, or at someone's home. Among peers drop to 잘 먹을게요. With close friends: 잘 먹을게. Skipping the phrase entirely when someone has cooked for you reads as rude or ungrateful in Korean culture.

잘 먹겠습니다 (before) vs 잘 먹었습니다 (after): the only difference is -겠- (forward) vs -었- (past). These are a pair; you need both in your repertoire. 맛있게 먹겠습니다 adds a compliment for the cook — warmer but less universal. There is no casual one-word alternative that carries the same gratitude; the phrase itself is the social act.
잘 먹겠습니다 (formal) → 잘 먹을게요 (polite-casual) → 잘 먹을게 (close friends) → 잘 먹자 (let's eat together, 반말 proposal). Warmer variant: 맛있게 먹겠습니다. After eating: 잘 먹었습니다 → 잘 먹었어요 → 잘 먹었어 (casual).

English speakers sometimes skip this phrase because English has no direct equivalent, or they interpret it as a weird vow about appetite and hesitate to say it for a small portion. Neither is right — 잘 먹겠습니다 is a fixed courtesy formula like 'bon appétit' crossed with 'thank you for the food', and you say it for any meal someone offers, no matter how small.

mistakes: Saying 잘 먹겠습니다 after finishing the meal — -겠- is forward-looking and only fits BEFORE eating; once done, switch to the past form 잘 먹었습니다.
Skipping it entirely when someone treats or cooks for you — omitting the pre-meal phrase in Korea reads as ungrateful; always say it at a hosted meal.

Interpreting it as a literal promise about appetite ('I will eat a lot / I will eat well') and avoiding it when not very hungry — it is a fixed social courtesy, not a statement of intention about food quantity.

usage: thanks, that was a great meal
polite (합쇼체) — right after finishing, especially to whoever cooked or paid
softer polite version (해요체) — everyday meals, warm but not stiff
complimenting the food and cook after eating — 맛있게 adds a flavor-specific warmth
thanks for the meal; next one's on me
standard gracious response after being treated — reciprocity is the social glue
examples: A: 어떠셨어요? / B: 정말 맛있었어요. 잘 먹었습니다.
A: How was it? / B: It was really delicious. Thank you for the meal.
natural end-of-meal exchange — B wraps up with the post-meal phrase after praising the food
A: 더 드실래요? / B: 아니요, 괜찮아요. 잘 먹었습니다.
A: Would you like more? / B: No, I'm good. Thank you, I ate well.
declining more food while still expressing gratitude — 잘 먹었습니다 closes the offer gracefully
사장님, 정말 잘 먹었습니다. 다음엔 제가 꼭 대접할게요.
Thank you so much for the meal, boss. Next time I'll absolutely treat you.
thanking whoever paid and immediately offering reciprocity — socially expected after a generous meal
nuance: 잘 먹었습니다 is the POST-meal thank-you, said as you finish, to whoever cooked or paid — functionally Korea's after-table 'that was a wonderful meal, thank you'. The only structural change from the pre-meal version is tense: 먹다 + past -었- + polite -습니다 = 'I ate well', versus the forward-looking 먹겠습니다. These two form an inseparable pair — 잘 먹겠습니다 at the start, 잘 먹었습니다 at the end — and learners who know only one half of the pair are conspicuously incomplete. Vowel note: 먹 + 었 → 먹었 (pronounced roughly '머거씀니다' due to linking); 먹었었 (double past) is grammatically possible but implies the eating is a discontinued past habit, which sounds unnatural here. Register: 잘 먹었습니다 (formal) → 잘 먹었어요 (polite-casual) → 잘 먹었어 (close friends). The English-speaker pitfall is treating it as a neutral factual report ('I have eaten') and therefore saying it to no one in particular, or just standing up and leaving — in Korean culture, always direct it to the host or treater, and the social expectation after being treated is to follow with 다음엔 제가 살게요 / 대접할게요 to signal future reciprocity.

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 잘 ('well') + 먹었습니다 ('I ate', past -었-). Real meaning: 'Thank you for the meal / that was wonderful' — a socially obligatory post-meal thank-you directed at whoever fed you, not a neutral factual statement.

Say it immediately after finishing, directed to whoever cooked or paid. Always address a specific person — not the room. Register: 잘 먹었습니다 (합쇼체) for any senior, elder, or formal setting. 잘 먹었어요 (해요체) for everyday polite use. 잘 먹었어 (반말) for friends. After being treated, follow up with 다음엔 제가 살게요 to show reciprocal intention.

잘 먹겠습니다 (before) vs 잘 먹었습니다 (after): -겠- = forward intention, -었- = completed past. These are a paired set. 맛있게 먹었습니다 adds flavor-appreciation ('I ate it deliciously'), which compliments the cook's skill more specifically. Saying 맛있었어요 ('it was delicious') is an additional comment but doesn't replace the post-meal courtesy formula.
잘 먹었습니다 (formal) → 잘 먹었어요 (polite) → 잘 먹었어 (casual). Expanded form: 정말 잘 먹었습니다. Pairing: 잘 먹었습니다 + 다음엔 제가 살게요 / 대접할게요. Food-specific compliment: 맛있게 먹었습니다 / 너무 맛있었어요.

Treating it as a factual 'I have eaten' and saying it to no one — or just leaving the table silently. In Korean table culture, 잘 먹었습니다 is a social obligation directed at the host or treater. Omitting it reads as rude; saying it to the air rather than a person undermines its social function.

mistakes: Saying 잘 먹겠습니다 after the meal — -겠- is forward-looking and belongs BEFORE eating; once you've eaten, the past form 잘 먹었습니다 is required.
Treating it as a neutral factual statement and directing it to no one — it is a thank-you and must be addressed to whoever cooked or paid, not announced into the room.
Using the double-past 먹었었습니다 — single past 잘 먹었습니다 is correct; the double past -었었- implies a discontinued or recalled habit and sounds unnatural in this fixed courtesy phrase.

usage: formal/business reunion — stepping up from 이에요 to 입니다
casual 반말, only with close friends or equals younger than you
it's been ages — have you been well?
natural two-part reunion opener: acknowledge the gap + ask how they've been
examples: A: 어, 지민 씨! 오랜만이에요. / B: 그러게요, 정말 오랜만이에요. 잘 지내셨어요?
A: Oh, Jimin! Long time no see. / B: I know, it really has been a while. Have you been well?
textbook reunion exchange — B echoes with 그러게요 ('I know, right') and mirrors the greeting before asking how A has been
민수 씨, 오랜만이에요. 그동안 어떻게 지냈어요?
Minsu, long time no see. How have you been all this time?
pairs 오랜만이에요 with the past-tense 지냈어요? to ask about the intervening period
어머, 이게 얼마 만이에요! 정말 오랜만이에요!
Oh my, how long has it been! It really has been ages!
surprised, emotional reunion — 이게 얼마 만이에요! ('how long has it been!') adds extra feeling before the main phrase
nuance: 오랜만이에요 is what you say when meeting someone after a meaningful gap in time. It comes from 오래 'a long time' + the particle 만 'an interval / it has been' (short for 간만에 'after an interval'), contracted and adjectivized into 오랜만, plus the polite copula 이에요 — literally 'it is (after) a long while'. The gap must feel genuinely long to the speakers; using it after only a few days or a week sounds ironic or sarcastic — Koreans occasionally joke 오랜만이네? about a friend they literally just saw yesterday. Spelling caution: it is 오랜만 (오래 + ㄴ + 만), NOT 오랫만, which is a common misspelling even by native speakers. Register slides from 반말 오랜만이야 → polite 오랜만이에요 → formal 오랜만입니다. The expression functions as an opener, not a standalone conversation — it naturally and almost obligatorily flows into 잘 지냈어요? ('have you been well?') or 그동안 어떻게 지냈어요? ('how have you been all this time?'). The echo reply is 저도요 ('me too') or 그러게요, 오랜만이에요 ('I know, it really has been').

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 오랜만 ('after a long interval', from 오래 'long time' + 만 'interval') + 이에요 (polite copula 'it is'). Real meaning: 'Long time no see' — acknowledging that a significant amount of time has passed since your last encounter. It is a copula sentence (not a verb sentence), which surprises English speakers expecting 'see'.

Use only when the time since your last meeting feels noticeably long — weeks, months, years. Register: 오랜만이야 (반말, close friends/equals) → 오랜만이에요 (해요체, polite peers) → 오랜만입니다 (합쇼체, formal). Almost always followed by 잘 지냈어요? or 그동안 어떻게 지냈어요? — launching straight into business after 오랜만이에요 without any check-in can feel cold.

오랜만이에요 vs 만나서 반가워요: the former is for REUNIONS (you've met before); the latter is strictly for FIRST meetings. Using 만나서 반가워요 at a reunion implies you forgot meeting the person. 오랜만이에요 vs 久しぶりです: functionally near-identical to the Japanese expression, and interestingly both evolved from similar cultural norms.
오랜만이야 (반말) → 오랜만이에요 (polite) → 오랜만입니다 (formal). Emotional intensifier: 정말 오랜만이에요 / 너무 오랜만이에요. Exclamatory opener: 이게 얼마 만이에요! ('how long has it been!'). Combined phrase: 정말 오랜만이에요, 잘 지냈어요?

Two traps: (1) Spelling it 오랫만이에요 — the correct spelling is 오랜만 (오래 + ㄴ만); 오랫 (with ㅅ) is wrong, though common. (2) Using it sarcastically after a short absence — it requires a real gap, or it comes across as ironic. A few days or a week is too short; the phrase needs to feel emotionally true.

mistakes: Spelling it 오랫만이에요 — the correct spelling is 오랜만이에요 (from 오래 + ㄴ + 만); 오랫만 with ㅅ is a very common error even among native speakers but is grammatically wrong.
Using it after only a short separation — 오랜만이에요 implies a real lapse of meaningful time; after a couple of days it sounds sarcastic or ironic.
Saying just 오랜만 to someone you should be polite to — the 이에요/이야 copula ending cannot be dropped for people you owe politeness; always say the full 오랜만이에요 or 오랜만입니다.

usage: polite open-ended check-in — asks about life lately, not just this moment
simpler, very common yes/no-style alternative — fishes for the reassuring 네, 잘 지내요
add 시 to show respect toward a senior, elder, or someone you address formally
explicitly scoped to 요즘 ('these days') — signals genuine interest in their recent life
examples: A: 오랜만이에요! 어떻게 지내셨어요? / B: 잘 지냈어요. 덕분에요. 민수 씨는요?
A: Long time no see! How have you been? / B: I've been well, thanks to you. And you, Minsu?
classic reunion exchange — B uses the polite 덕분에요 ('thanks to you, I'm well') and bounces the question back
그동안 어떻게 지냈어요? 많이 바빴어요?
How have you been all this time? Were you very busy?
past 지냈어요 scopes to the period since you last met — natural follow-up at a reunion
A: 요즘 어떻게 지내세요? / B: 그냥 그래요. 별로 특별한 건 없어요.
A: How are things these days? / B: So-so. Nothing particularly special.
honorific form for a senior, and an honest non-formulaic reply using 그냥 그래요 ('so-so')
nuance: 어떻게 지내요? asks how someone has been LIVING and getting on lately — it looks back over a stretch of days, not at this one moment. 어떻게 = 'how / in what way'; 지내다 = 'to get by, to spend one's days, to live (in a day-to-day sense)'. This is NOT a question about someone's physical location (confusable with 가다 'to go') or emotional state right now — it's about the texture of their recent life. The nearest synonym 잘 지내요? is a simpler yes/no probe: it asks IF they're doing well, while 어떻게 지내요? asks HOW, inviting a more open answer. Register is scalable: base polite 지내요 → honorific 지내세요 for seniors. Tense shift: present 지내요? is a general 'how are you?'; past 지냈어요? scopes to 'how have you been (since we last met)?' and fits naturally after 오랜만이에요. The expected answers are not just 네 — socially you offer a brief update (잘 지내요 / 그냥 그래요 / 바빴어요) and then return the question (민수 씨는요? / 어떠세요?).

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 어떻게 ('how / in what way') + 지내요 ('are you getting by / living your days', from 지내다 'to spend/pass time'). Real meaning: 'How have you been lately?' — a check-in on the general quality of someone's recent life, not a question about their current location or immediate feeling.

Appropriate at reunions, as a conversation opener after 오랜만이에요, or simply as a warm check-in with someone you haven't spoken to recently. 어떻게 지내요? (해요체) for peers and polite strangers. 어떻게 지내세요? (honorific) for seniors, teachers, in-laws. A bare 어떻게 지내? is casual 반말, only for close friends or those younger than you.

어떻게 지내요? ('how are you getting on?') is open-ended, inviting a real answer. 잘 지내요? ('are you doing well?') is a narrower yes/no question that expects 네, 잘 지내요. 어떻게 지내요? allows for honest 그냥 그래요 ('so-so') or 좀 힘들었어요 ('it's been a bit tough') without social awkwardness — it's a real question, not just a greeting filler.

어떻게 지내요? (present, general) → 어떻게 지냈어요? (past, since we last met) → 요즘 어떻게 지내요? (scoped to these days) → 어떻게 지내세요? (honorific). Expected replies: 잘 지내요 (doing well) / 그냥 그래요 (so-so) / 덕분에 잘 지내요 (well, thanks to you). Follow-up: 정말요? 뭔가 특별한 일이 있었어요?

Two traps: (1) Confusing 지내요 with 가요 ('going') because 지내다 and 가다 can both vaguely suggest movement — 지내다 means 'to live/get by', not 'to go somewhere'; answer about HOW you ARE, not WHERE you go. (2) Replying with a bare 네 — 어떻게 지내요? invites a short content answer and a reciprocal question; a naked 네 reads as dismissive.

mistakes: Confusing 지내요 with 가요 and answering with a destination — 지내다 means 'to get by / to live (day to day)', so reply about life quality (잘 지내요, 그냥 그래요), not about where you are going.
Replying with only a bare 네 — 어떻게 지내요? invites a brief real answer and a reciprocal question; always add at least 잘 지내요 and ideally bounce it back with 민수 씨는요?
Asking a clearly senior person 어떻게 지내? in casual 반말 — for anyone you should address formally, use the honorific 어떻게 지내세요? to show appropriate respect.

usage: warm, friendly-polite (해요체) — for peers and acquaintances on happy news
formal occasions: award ceremonies, company announcements, official events
toward a senior or elder — 드리다 'to give (humbly)' shows deference
highest register of sincerity: 진심으로 ('from the heart') + humble 드립니다
examples: A: 시험에 합격했어요! / B: 정말요? 축하해요! 고생했어요.
A: I passed the exam! / B: Really? Congratulations! You worked so hard.
immediate spontaneous reaction to good news — 고생했어요 acknowledges the effort behind the achievement
졸업 축하해요! 앞날이 더 빛날 거예요.
Congratulations on your graduation! Your future will be even brighter.
occasion word 졸업 fronts the phrase — the standard [occasion] + 축하해요 pattern; warm wish follows
부장님, 승진을 진심으로 축하드립니다. 앞으로도 잘 부탁드리겠습니다.
Director, I offer my sincere congratulations on your promotion. I look forward to your continued guidance.
humble 축하드리다 toward a clearly senior person; followed by 잘 부탁드리겠습니다 to reinforce deference
nuance: 축하해요 congratulates someone on genuinely HAPPY news. 축하(祝賀) is Sino-Korean — 祝 'to wish, to celebrate' + 賀 'to congratulate' — and it conjugates as a 하다-verb: 축하하다 → 축하해요 (polite) → 축하합니다 (formal) → 축하해 (casual). The structural pattern is [occasion noun] + 축하해요: 결혼 축하해요, 합격 축하해요, 생일 축하해요, 출산 축하해요. Register is critical: toward a senior, use the humble 축하드려요 / 축하드립니다 (드리다 'to give humbly'), NOT plain 축하해요, because you are offering the congratulation upward as a gift rather than stating it. The English-speaker pitfall is using 축하해요 like the broad English 'congratulations' — in Korean, 축하 is strictly for joyful milestones. For someone going through hardship (failed exam, difficult project, loss) you never 축하; you say 힘내세요 ('stay strong'), 고생했어요 ('you worked hard'), or offer 수고 language. Also, don't conflate with 화이팅 — 화이팅 cheers someone ON before they face a challenge; 축하해요 celebrates AFTER the good outcome has arrived.

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 축하(祝賀) ('congratulation', Sino-Korean) + 해요 (polite 하다-verb ending). Real meaning: 'Congratulations' — strictly for happy milestones where the news is objectively joyful. Not a general 'well done' for any effortful situation, and never appropriate for hardship.

Use ONLY for genuinely happy news: births, weddings, graduations, promotions, job offers, awards, passing exams. Register: 축하해 (반말, close friends) → 축하해요 (해요체, peers) → 축하합니다 (합쇼체, formal ceremonies) → 축하드려요/축하드립니다 (humble, toward seniors). The humble 드리다 form is not optional when congratulating someone senior to you.

축하해요 vs 화이팅: 화이팅 is a pre-challenge cheer ('you can do it!'); 축하해요 is a post-success celebration. 축하해요 vs 고생했어요: 고생했어요 ('you worked hard') acknowledges effort without celebrating an outcome — more neutral-sympathetic, usable for both successes and hard times. Pairing them: 축하해요! 정말 고생했어요 ('congratulations! you really worked so hard') is natural and warm.
축하해 (반말) → 축하해요 (polite) → 축하합니다 (formal) → 축하드려요 (humble). Intensified: 진심으로 축하해요 / 정말 축하해요. Occasion pattern: [event] + 축하해요 — 생일 축하해요, 졸업 축하해요, 합격 축하해요, 결혼 축하해요.

English 'congratulations' is used broadly — even for completing something difficult or unpleasant. Korean 축하해요 is strictly for happy outcomes. Using it when someone just survived a brutal project or got through a hard time comes across as tone-deaf. For effort without guaranteed joy, use 고생했어요 or 수고했어요 instead.

mistakes: Using 축하해요 for difficult or sorrowful situations — it is only for genuinely happy news; for someone who went through hardship say 힘내세요 or 고생했어요 instead.
Saying plain 축하해요 to a clearly senior person — toward elders, bosses, or respected seniors, the humble form 축하드려요 / 축하드립니다 is expected and its omission can seem disrespectful.
Mixing it up with 화이팅 — 화이팅 cheers someone on BEFORE a challenge; 축하해요 celebrates AFTER the good outcome has arrived. Using 축하해요 before someone takes an exam would be bizarre and presumptuous.

usage: warm, friendly-polite (해요체) — peer, coworker, new acquaintance
formal occasions or when you want an extra layer of respect with a peer at work; the birthday-song lyric
casual 반말 — to a close friend of equal or younger age
to parents, grandparents, teachers, elders — both the NOUN (생일→생신) and the VERB (해요→드려요) must be upgraded
examples: A: 오늘 제 생일이에요! / B: 정말요? 생일 축하해요! 소원 빌었어요?
A: Today is my birthday! / B: Really? Happy birthday! Did you make a wish?
spontaneous natural reaction — 소원 빌었어요? ('did you make a wish?') is a culturally warm follow-up
민수 씨, 생일 축하해요. 건강하고 좋은 일만 가득하길 바라요.
Minsu, happy birthday. I hope you're healthy and filled with only good things.
adds a warm wish after the greeting — 좋은 일만 가득하길 바라요 is a very common Korean birthday wish phrase
할머니, 생신 축하드려요. 오래오래 건강하세요.
Grandma, happy birthday. Please stay healthy for a very long time.
BOTH words upgraded: 생신 (honorific noun) + 축하드려요 (humble verb) — the full respectful birthday greeting for an elder
nuance: 생일 축하해요 = 생일(生日) 'birthday' (Sino-Korean: 生 birth + 日 day) + 축하해요 'congratulations'. Korean 'congratulates' a birthday rather than wishing it 'happy' — a useful mismatch from English 'happy birthday'. The register layering is the most important lesson: there are TWO things you must change for elders, not just one. The NOUN upgrades from 생일 (general) to 생신 (honorific form of 생일, used only for respected elders). The VERB upgrades from 축하해요 (polite) to 축하드려요/드립니다 (humble-deferential). Getting only one right but not both — e.g. 생신 축하해요 or 생일 축하드려요 — is a half-measure that still sounds under-polite. The full register ladder: 생일 축하해 (friend/반말) → 생일 축하해요 (polite peer, 해요체) → 생일 축하합니다 (formal) → 생신 축하드려요/드립니다 (elder, humble). The famous birthday song uses 생일 축하합니다 (four times). The English-speaker pitfall is treating birthday greetings as one-size-fits-all, not realizing Korean requires you to match BOTH the noun and the verb to the recipient's status.

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 생일(生日) ('birthday', Sino-Korean) + 축하해요 ('congratulations'). Real meaning: 'Happy birthday' — but the Korean phrase 'congratulates' rather than wishes 'happiness'. This is a small but memorable structural difference from English that helps learners remember the phrase.

The noun AND verb must both match the recipient's status. Peer or friend: 생일 축하해요 / 생일 축하해. Elder (parents, grandparents, teacher): 생신 축하드려요 / 생신 축하드립니다. Getting the noun right but the verb wrong (생신 축하해요) still misses the full register. The birthday song uses 생일 축하합니다 — always heard in a group sing.

생일 축하해요 vs 생신 축하드려요: same occasion, but the noun (생일 → 생신) and verb (해요 → 드려요) BOTH must change for elders — not just one. 생일 축하해요 to a grandparent isn't catastrophic but sounds under-polite and childish. Adding a birthday wish: 좋은 하루 보내세요 ('have a great day') or 건강하세요 ('stay healthy') naturally follows the birthday greeting.

생일 축하해 (반말) → 생일 축하해요 (polite) → 생일 축하합니다 (formal/song) → 생신 축하드려요 (humble, elder) → 생신 축하드립니다 (formal-humble, elder). Common follow-on wishes: 건강하세요, 소원이 이루어지길 바라요 ('I hope your wish comes true'), 좋은 하루 보내세요.

English 'happy birthday' is register-neutral — one phrase for everyone from a best friend to a grandparent. Korean requires upgrading BOTH the noun (생일 → 생신) and the verb (해요 → 드려요) for elders. Upgrading only one half is still incorrect. Many English speakers also try to translate 'happy' into Korean (행복한 생일?), but Korean uses 축하 (congratulate), never a 'happy' equivalent in birthday greetings.

mistakes: Using 생일 instead of the honorific 생신 for elders — to parents, grandparents, or respected seniors, say 생신 축하드려요; 생일 축하해요 sounds childish and under-polite in this context.
Pairing honorific 생신 with plain 축하해요 — the upgrade must apply to BOTH the noun (생일→생신) AND the verb (해요→드려요); 생신 축하해요 is a half-measure that still misses the mark.
Trying to add a 'happy' word (행복한 생일, 즐거운 생일) — Korean uses 축하 ('congratulate') for birthdays, not an equivalent of 'happy'; there is no such phrase in standard Korean birthday greetings.

english: Thank you for your hard work.
usage: thank you for your hard work
formal (합쇼체 + honorific) — after completed work, best from a superior or peer, not directed upward
softer polite version (해요체) — same situation, slightly less formal
present tense — to someone STILL working as you depart; this is NOT the same phrase as 하셨습니다
thank you for all your hard effort
warmer near-synonym — 고생 ('hardship/toil') feels more heartfelt about the difficulty endured than 수고
examples: A: 발표 정말 수고하셨습니다. 덕분에 잘 됐어요. / B: 감사합니다. 열심히 준비했습니다.
A: You really worked hard on that presentation. It went great thanks to you. / B: Thank you. I prepared hard for it.
supervisor (A) thanks the presenter (B) after the presentation — 수고하셨습니다 flows naturally downward from A to B after completed work
오늘 회의 수고하셨습니다. 내일 뵙겠습니다.
Thank you for your work in today's meeting. See you tomorrow.
wrapping up a meeting — 수고하셨습니다 marks the task as finished; pairs with the next-meeting farewell
A: 다들 수고하세요. 저 먼저 퇴근합니다. / B: 네, 안녕히 가세요.
A: Everyone, keep at it. I'm heading home first. / B: Yes, take care. Goodbye.
present-tense 수고하세요 directed at colleagues who are still working — notice the tense difference from 하셨습니다
nuance: 수고하셨습니다 acknowledges finished effort. 수고(受苦 / loosely) means 'trouble, effort, hard work'; 하시— is the honorific stem of 하다 'to do'; and the past -셨- marks completion, so the phrase means '(you) have done hard work'. The make-or-break contrast is TENSE and DIRECTION. Tense: 수고하셨습니다 (past, work is finished) vs 수고하세요 (present, person is still at it — used as you leave). Mix these and you are either congratulating someone mid-task or urging a finished person to keep going. Direction: 수고하셨습니다 flows naturally downward (superior to junior) or sideways (peers), but upward to a clearly senior boss it can sound presumptuous, as if you are evaluating their effort from a position of authority you don't have — to a superior, 감사합니다 or 고생 많으셨습니다 is safer. The near-synonym 고생하셨습니다 (고생 'hardship/toil') feels warmer and more empathetic about the difficulty of the work, not just the fact of effort. Casual register: 수고했어 (반말, to a junior or close peer). The English-speaker pitfall is conflating it with a casual 'thanks' and dropping it on anyone regardless of rank or whether the work is done.

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 수고 ('trouble/effort') + 하셨습니다 ('you did', honorific past). Real meaning: 'Thank you for your hard work' — a verbal acknowledgment of completed effort, directed at the person who performed it. Not a casual 'thanks' for any small favor; it specifically recognizes sustained effort or a task now finished.

Use after the work is DONE: after a meeting, at end of shift, after a presentation. Direction matters: supervisor-to-junior or peer-to-peer is natural. Upward to a clearly senior boss risks sounding presumptuous — use 감사합니다 or 고생 많으셨습니다 for superiors. Register: 수고하셨습니다 (formal) → 수고하셨어요 (polite-casual) → 수고했어 (반말, junior/close peer).

수고하셨습니다 vs 수고하세요: completely different situations — 하셨습니다 is past (work done); 하세요 is present (work ongoing, said as you leave). 수고하셨습니다 vs 고생하셨습니다: both acknowledge effort, but 고생 (hardship/toil) implies the work was genuinely difficult and tough; 수고 is more neutral. Either fits after demanding tasks; 고생하셨습니다 is slightly warmer and more emotionally resonant.
수고했어 (반말, casual) → 수고하셨어요 (polite) → 수고하셨습니다 (formal). Present tense set: 수고해 / 수고하세요 (keep at it). Warmer synonyms: 고생하셨습니다 / 고생 많으셨습니다 ('you endured great hardship'). Intensified: 정말 수고하셨습니다.

Two traps: (1) Directing it upward to a boss as if it were a neutral 'thanks' — it can imply you are judging or evaluating their effort from a superior position; for a senior use 감사합니다 or 고생 많으셨습니다 carefully. (2) Confusing the tense — 수고하셨습니다 is only for FINISHED work; 수고하세요 is for work STILL IN PROGRESS. Mixing these is the most common learner tense error with this phrase.

mistakes: Saying 수고하셨습니다 upward to a clearly higher-ranking boss — directed upward it can sound presumptuous, as if you are evaluating their effort; to a superior use 감사합니다 or 고생 많으셨습니다 with care.
Confusing the tenses — 수고하셨습니다 is for FINISHED work; if the person is still working, the present-tense 수고하세요 is the correct phrase.
Using casual 반말 수고했어 with someone you owe politeness to — that form is only for juniors or close peers; otherwise keep 수고하셨습니다 or at least 수고하셨어요.

usage: friendly-polite (해요체) — suitable for peers, partners, friends you address with 요; NOT for elders
casual 반말 — close friends, a partner, family members younger than you
to parents, grandparents, teachers, respected seniors — uses the suppletive honorific verb 주무시다
warm add-on for any register — 꿔요 is polite, 꾸세요 is honorific, 꿔 is casual
examples: A: 이제 자야 할 것 같아요. 잘 자요. / B: 네, 잘 자요. 좋은 꿈 꿔요.
A: I think I need to sleep now. Good night. / B: Good night. Sweet dreams.
a nighttime farewell between peers — both mirror the greeting and B adds a warm sweet-dreams wish
늦었네요. 내일 일찍 일어나야 해요. 잘 자요.
It's getting late. I have to wake up early tomorrow. Good night.
natural parting at the end of an evening — the reason for leaving makes the farewell feel authentic, not abrupt
엄마, 아빠, 안녕히 주무세요. 좋은 꿈 꾸세요.
Mom, Dad, good night. Sweet dreams.
honorific 주무세요 for parents — both the sleep verb AND the dream-wish use the honorific 꾸세요 form
nuance: 잘 자요 = 잘 'well' + 자요 (polite imperative of 자다 'to sleep'), literally 'sleep well'. It is friendly-polite, sitting in the 해요체 register, and is warm for peers, partners, and friends. However, it is NOT respectful enough for elders, parents, grandparents, or anyone you owe significant social deference — to them you must switch to the entirely different honorific verb 주무시다 (the suppletive honorific of 자다), giving 안녕히 주무세요 ('please sleep peacefully'). This verb-swapping is the core of the lesson — exactly parallel to 먹다 → 드시다, 있다 → 계시다, 자다 → 주무시다 — Korean has suppletive honorific verbs for basic bodily and daily actions. Trying to 'make it polite' with extra endings (잘 자세요) does not work because 자세요 is a SLIGHTLY softer polite request form but still uses the plain verb 자다, not the honorific 주무시다. The English-speaker pitfall is applying the one-size-fits-all 'good night' mindset to 잘 자요 and saying it to a grandparent or a boss — it sounds overly familiar, almost like telling your CEO to 'catch some Z's'. Decision rule: intimate or peer level → 잘 자(요); elder or superior → 안녕히 주무세요. The sweet-dreams add-on 좋은 꿈 꿔요/꾸세요 matches the register of the main phrase.

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 잘 ('well') + 자요 ('sleep', polite imperative of 자다). Real meaning: 'Good night / sleep well' — a bedtime farewell. It is both a wish and a farewell; saying it implies the conversation or meeting is ending and the recipient is heading to sleep.

Use ONLY at or near bedtime — it is not a general daytime farewell. Decision by relationship: close friend or peer → 잘 자요 / 잘 자; elder (parent, grandparent, teacher, respected senior) → 안녕히 주무세요 / 주무십시오. You cannot fix 잘 자요 for elders by changing endings (잘 자세요 still uses the plain verb). The suppletive verb 주무시다 is the only correct upgrade.
chips: DO NOT: 잘 자세요 for elders

structuredNuance.t: 잘 자요 (peer) vs 안녕히 주무세요 (elder): the distinction is not register endings but the VERB itself — 자다 vs 주무시다 are suppletive pairs. 잘 자요 vs 좋은 꿈 꿔요: the latter is an add-on sweet-dreams wish, not a replacement for the main farewell. 잘 자요 vs 안녕히 계세요/가세요: those are general goodbyes for any time of day; 잘 자요 is exclusively nighttime.

잘 자 (반말) → 잘 자요 (polite) → 안녕히 주무세요 (honorific). Add-ons: 좋은 꿈 꿔 (casual) / 좋은 꿈 꿔요 (polite) / 좋은 꿈 꾸세요 (honorific). Extra warmth: 몸조리 잘 하세요 ('take care of yourself'). The full elder version: 안녕히 주무세요. 좋은 꿈 꾸세요.

English 'good night' is register-neutral — you say it to your boss and your best friend identically. 잘 자요 is NOT neutral; it is an intimate peer-level phrase. Saying it to an elder or a boss sounds as out-of-place as calling your manager 'buddy' at the end of the workday. The fix requires a different VERB (주무시다), not just a fancier ending.

mistakes: Saying 잘 자요 to an elder or boss — it is too familiar; the honorific fix requires the suppletive verb 주무시다, giving 안녕히 주무세요, not just a politer ending on 자다.
Trying to make 자다 respectful for elders by saying 잘 자세요 — 자세요 still uses the plain verb 자다, not the required honorific 주무시다; the only correct elder form is 안녕히 주무세요.
Using 잘 자요 as a daytime parting — it specifically wishes sleep and only fits at bedtime or when someone is heading to bed; as a general daytime goodbye use 안녕히 가세요 / 안녕히 계세요 instead.
